articles.author: Stuart S
articles.description:
For years my projects page was a wall of text. Names, dates, a line each. Accurate, and completely forgettable - you can't tell a dashboard I'm proud of from a site I've half-forgotten when they're both one grey sentence.
So I rebuilt it around screenshots. It now leads with a few case studies - a hero shot, a strip of thumbnails, the story beside it - then a fuller catalogue you can open a line at a time. Click any image and it opens full-size; arrow or swipe through the rest.
Here's the snag, and it's the interesting bit: most of my best work is internal. The backoffice a whole casino runs on, the tool that publishes artwork across twelve thousand games - nobody outside ever sees them, and I can't hand you a login. For a long time that's exactly why the page stayed a list. If you can't show it, why try?
The answer was to show it anyway, honestly: screenshots of the internal tools with the sensitive data blurred, the games that are public, the side projects that aren't finished yet, and a plain "type-only" line where something genuinely can't be shown. "I built this, and here's what it looked like" beats "I built this" every time, even when there's no URL to click.
Under the hood it discovers its own screenshots - drop an image in a folder, it appears, no lists to maintain - and the page still scores 100 on Lighthouse. But the lesson wasn't technical. If your best work lives behind a login, don't let that argue you out of a portfolio. Show what you can, say plainly what you can't, and let the pictures make the case.
articles.title: When your best work is behind a login

Preface
ACAI is proposed as a modular architecture intended to organize cognitive functions into specialized components. Instead of increasing parameter count alone, ACAI aims to improve reasoning quality, maintainability, transparency, and engineering flexibility.
Instead of solving these issues by increasing model size alone, ACAI proposes a layered architecture in which different components cooperate to perform specialized cognitive tasks. This design philosophy is inspired by systems engineering principles: divide responsibilities into well-defined modules, allow independent improvement of each component, and coordinate them through a structured workflow.

articles.description:
Feature flags are easy to add and hard to remove. That asymmetry is where the trouble starts.
Used properly, feature flags give you safer deployments, gradual rollouts, and emergency kill switches. Used poorly, they turn your codebase into a haunted house full of dead branches nobody dares to touch.
Here are some of the most common ways feature flags go wrong.
A zombie flag is a flag that should have been deleted months ago but wasn't.
The feature shipped. The experiment ended. Everyone moved on. But the flag?
Still there.
Nobody remembers what it does, why it exists, or whether removing it will summon Cthulhu.
Zombie flags accumulate over time. Eventually your codebase is full of if statements that will never execute, conditions that are always true, and dead code paths nobody has tested …
articles.title: Feature Flag Pitfalls: How to Turn Your Codebase Into a Haunted House

Nothing here is a client’s data, and the site is not named. It is a Next.js application on Node behind a reverse proxy, and a worked example of how a modern site is actually attacked, and how building it carefully answered that.

articles.description:
Why do teams use feature flags?
Because "move fast and break things" is only fun until you break prod.
Feature flags let you move fast and break things slightly less dramatically.
Here’s how real engineering teams actually use them.
A canary release means you roll out a change to a small percentage of users first—say, 1%—before exposing it to everyone.
If the 1% starts screaming, you flip the flag off and investigate.
If they don't notice anything wrong, you gradually increase the rollout.
The name comes from the old mining practice of bringing a canary into a coal mine to detect toxic gases.
Your early users are the canary.
Hopefully, nothing explodes.
This pattern is especially valuable for high-traffic systems where even a small bug can affect thousands of users. Rolling out slowly give…
articles.title: Feature Flags in the Real World: Use Cases That Won't Get You Fired
